IL	Mentorship stands as a cornerstone for personal and professional growth, offering guidance,
wisdom, and inspiration. A mentor transcends the roles of teachers or coaches, embodying role
models and confidants who shape lives with their experience and dedication.
The significance of mentors in personal growth is profound. They guide critical life decisions,
challenge comfort zones, and foster self-confidence. By sharing life lessons, mentors equip
individuals with insights to navigate challenges and embrace new possibilities. Additionally,
mentors play pivotal roles in professional spheres, offering advice, networking opportunities, and
industry knowledge. Their guidance aids in career advancement, ensuring mentees achieve their
professional aspirations.
Beyond immediate benefits, effective mentoring yields lasting impacts, shaping values, beliefs,
and perspectives. Mentors bolster mental and emotional well-being, serving as trusted confidants
during life's challenges. Numerous successful individuals attribute their accomplishments to
mentorship, underscoring its enduring influence on personal and professional achievements.
For those aspiring to mentor or seek mentorship, compatibility remains paramount. Establishing
trust and understanding forms the bedrock of fruitful mentor-mentee relationships. Effective
mentors prioritize empowerment, encouraging critical thinking, decision-making, and
independence in their mentees. Rather than fostering dependencies, they equip mentees with tools
and confidence to thrive independently.
In essence, mentors illuminate paths toward self-discovery, growth, and success. Whether seeking
mentorship or cherishing existing relationships, recognizing the transformative power of
mentorship is crucial. By fostering knowledge, experience, and compassion, individuals can create
positive impacts, fostering growth, success, and fulfillment for themselves and others. Embracing
mentorship not only unlocks potential but also perpetuates a cycle of growth and inspiration,
enriching lives and communities alike.

questions.stimulus:
II.	Recently, a bhai sahib very nearly scrunched up his nose when he saw me break a chicken leg,
politely warning me that “you become what you eat.” If that were true, I almost told him, half of
India would have turned into samosas by now. The (not-so) gentleman went on about the violence
of killing, and how the emotions of animals were also being eaten by “you people.” I’ve run into
this often — our favourite yoga posture: Moral Superiority. Many among us look down upon meat-
eaters who supposedly contaminate not just their stomachs but their souls. Even onions and garlic
are accused of stirring up passions. It all comes from old spiritual lines of thought where food
wasn’t mere fuel but personality programming: sattvic foods made you serene, rajasic made you
ambitious, and tamasic made you sluggish or sinful. Meanwhile, we’ve spent centuries eating rice
and wheat, which have no qualities whatsoever except silently putting up with all our theories.
For many Indians, vegetarianism is not just diet — it’s identity, hierarchy, morality, sometimes
even politics. Yet this belief that a “gentle diet” equals non-violence is a pleasant myth. We love
discussing it between spoonfuls of ghee sourced from an industry that treats calves as collateral
damage. The hypocrisy runs deeper than a single industry. We draw a moral line at the individual
act of killing, yet we'll cheerfully destroy their homes for roads, farms, minerals, and malls, wiping
out insects, frogs, rodents, snakes, and small mammals by the millions every farming season.
Now imagine, for a reckless moment, a day on earth when the invisible scissors of predation go
still. Nothing stalks, hunts, pecks, gulps, stings, snaps, or digests. A 24-hour spiritual detox for the
food chain. A day when every creature, including you and me — the universe’s tiniest residents —
gets a ceasefire from the oldest war of all: life eating life.

gentle-living-in-a-predatory-world-10433706/

politely warning me that “you become what you eat.” If that were true, I almost told him, half of
India would have turned into samosas by now. The (not-so) gentleman went on about the violence
of killing, and how the emotions of animals were also being eaten by “you people.” I’ve run into
this often — our favourite yoga posture: Moral Superiority. Many among us look down upon meat-
eaters who supposedly contaminate not just their stomachs but their souls. Even onions and garlic
are accused of stirring up passions. It all comes from old spiritual lines of thought where food
wasn’t mere fuel but personality programming: sattvic foods made you serene, rajasic made you
ambitious, and tamasic made you sluggish or sinful. Meanwhile, we’ve spent centuries eating rice
and wheat, which have no qualities whatsoever except silently putting up with all our theories.
For many Indians, vegetarianism is not just diet — it’s identity, hierarchy, morality, sometimes
even politics. Yet this belief that a “gentle diet” equals non-violence is a pleasant myth. We love
discussing it between spoonfuls of ghee sourced from an industry that treats calves as collateral
damage. The hypocrisy runs deeper than a single industry. We draw a moral line at the individual
act of killing, yet we'll cheerfully destroy their homes for roads, farms, minerals, and malls, wiping
out insects, frogs, rodents, snakes, and small mammals by the millions every farming season.

still. Nothing stalks, hunts, pecks, gulps, stings, snaps, or digests. A 24-hour spiritual detox for the
food chain. A day when every creature, including you and me — the universe’s tiniest residents —
gets a ceasefire from the oldest war of all: life eating life.

questions.stimulus:
Ii.	The tension between individual freedom and collective responsibility is not just a political or legal
issue; it pervades every aspect of our lives, particularly when it comes to choices about food. Take
the debate around eating animals. On the one hand, the appetite for meat is deeply ingrained in
many cultures, driven by tradition, convenience, and sheer pleasure. On the other, the ethical
implications of killing animals for consumption raise serious questions. Philosophers, like Peter
Singer, argue that our moral obligation extends to all sentient beings, and that causing
unnecessary harm to animals is a violation of our ethical duty. Meanwhile, others contend that
eating animals is a natural and essential part of human life.
In this battle between the individual and the collective, the law often plays a decisive role. In
countries where the consumption of certain animals is controversial, legal systems step in to strike
a balance between cultural practices and ethical considerations. Some countries have enacted laws
that prohibit the slaughter of specific animals, citing animal rights and public health concerns,
while others defend the freedom to consume meat as a basic human right. Yet, the law's role is not

to make moral judgments but to establish the boundaries within which people can exercise their
freedom, preventing harm to others while respecting individual rights.www.lawpreptutorial.com
The concept of moral relativism also complicates this issue. What one culture considers acceptable
may be seen as unethical in another. In a pluralistic society, such differences must be navigated
with sensitivity and respect. In this way, the law serves as an imperfect mediator, guiding society
through ethical dilemmas without claiming to offer a perfect solution, yet ensuring that certain
moral principles—such as the prohibition of cruelty—remain non-negotiable.
Source: With edits from https://animalandmind.com/

IV.	In the bustling streets of New York City, a young woman named Elena found herself caught
between two worlds. On one hand, there was her career as a promising architect, where every
project was a step toward professional success. On the other, there was her deep yearning for
something more—something beyond the glass-and-steel skyscrapers she designed. For years, she
had lived by the rigid rules of ambition and competition, but recently, an unusual sense of
dissatisfaction had started to cloud her vision.
It wasn’t the kind of dissatisfaction that could be solved with a raise or a promotion. Elena was
tired of designing buildings that were impressive on paper but lifeless in spirit. She longed for
creative freedom, the kind that could only be found in art. Her sketches, once filled with geometric
precision, now overflowed with swirling lines and bold, vibrant colors—shapes that had no purpose
except to express an emotion she couldn’t name.
One evening, after a long day at the office, Elena walked to a nearby park. She sat by the fountain,
letting the sound of the water soothe her mind. As the sky began to darken, she took out her
sketchbook and began to draw without thinking. She didn’t care whether it was perfect or
practical. For the first time in years, Elena felt alive.
The city’s chaos seemed distant now. In the stillness of the park, she realized something profound:
It wasn’t success she sought, but authenticity. The answer had always been within her, waiting for
her to stop chasing after an ideal and embrace what truly mattered. And with that realization,
Elena began to feel a sense of peace she had never known before.

VI.	The Aravalli range represents one of the most ancient geological formations in the Indian
subcontinent and plays a critical ecological role in northern and western India. Stretching across
multiple states, the range functions as a natural barrier against desertification, supports
groundwater recharge and sustains diverse flora and fauna. Its environmental significance
extends to climate regulation, air quality improvement and soil conservation in densely populated
regions.
Over time, the Aravallis have faced increasing pressure from mining, urban expansion and
infrastructure development. These activities have resulted in habitat fragmentation, groundwater
depletion and loss of forest cover. In response, regulatory and judicial interventions have sought to
introduce scientific criteria for identifying ecologically sensitive areas and balancing conservation
with developmental needs.
Recent policy approaches emphasise landscape-level restoration, sustainable land-use planning
and inter-state coordination. Initiatives such as green corridors and afforestation programmes aim
to rehabilitate degraded stretches while strengthening ecological continuity. The use of geospatial
mapping and environmental impact assessments has gained importance in decision-making
processes.
However, challenges persist in harmonising economic interests with long-term environmental
sustainability. Differences in state-level implementation, definitional ambiguities and enforcement
gaps continue to influence outcomes. The Aravalli case highlights broader concerns regarding
environmental governance, judicial oversight and the need for science-based conservation
strategies in rapidly urbanising regions.

VIL. India’s rural employment framework has been central to addressing livelihood insecurity and
asset creation in rural areas. Over time, policy debates have emerged regarding the efficiency,
fiscal sustainability and developmental impact of existing employment guarantee models.
Concerns related to non-durable asset creation, labour market distortions and rising expenditure
have prompted discussions on restructuring rural employment schemes.
The proposed approach under the VB—-G RAM G framework seeks to integrate employment
generation with long-term infrastructure development and livelihood enhancement. Emphasis is
placed on creating durable assets aligned with national priorities such as water security, rural
connectivity and climate resilience. Planning mechanisms are designed to operate through local
institutions while remaining aligned with broader infrastructure strategies.
Fiscal restructuring forms an important component, with a shift towards defined allocations and
shared responsibility between the Centre and States. Digital platforms and data-driven planning
tools aim to improve transparency, monitoring and convergence with other development
programmes. Seasonal flexibility in implementation is intended to reduce conflicts with
agricultural labour demand.
The framework reflects a broader shift from welfare-oriented employment provision to
productivity-linked rural development. At the same time, its effectiveness depends on institutional
capacity, coordination across governance levels and the ability to balance social protection with
economic efficiency in rural policy design.

SECTION II
X.	The doctrine of proportionality has increasingly been used by Indian courts to test the validity of
State action that restricts fundamental rights. The doctrine requires that any restriction imposed
by the State must pursue a legitimate aim, must be suitable to achieve that aim, must be
necessary in the sense that no less restrictive alternative is available, and must maintain a proper
balance between the extent of restriction and the importance of the objective sought to be
achieved.
In Modern Dental College v. State of Madhya Pradesh, the Supreme Court clarified that
proportionality is an essential part of constitutional adjudication under Articles 19 and 21. Later,
in Puttaswamy v. Union of India, the Court expanded the application of proportionality to privacy-
related claims, holding that even a law enacted by Parliament can be struck down if it fails the
proportionality test.
However, the Court has also recognized that in matters involving national security, public order,
and economic regulation, the legislature and executive are entitled to a certain degree of
deference. This does not mean that judicial review is excluded, but that courts must be cautious
not to substitute their own judgment for that of the elected branches unless the restriction is
manifestly arbitrary or excessive.
Thus, proportionality operates as a balancing tool that neither grants unchecked power to the
State nor absolute freedom to individuals, but seeks to harmonize individual rights with collective
interests in a constitutional democracy.

governed by the Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) and include theft, extortion, robbery,

or loss may be relevant to determining the extent of liability.

authorization can absolve the accused if the act was permitted. Mistake of fact may serve as a
defense if the accused reasonably believed they had the right to the property. Additionally, duress
or coercion may be considered in specific circumstances, particularly when the act was committed
under threat.

offences involving digital assets. Courts often consider the intention, mode of commission, value of

of offences and defenses, Indian criminal law ensures protection of property rights while balancing
fairness and social order.

XII. Comparative International Law studies how different countries structure and enforce legal rules
and principles in areas such as treaties, human rights, commercial law, and dispute resolution. It
involves analyzing domestic legal systems, international conventions, and customary practices to
understand similarities and differences in lawmaking, interpretation, and enforcement across
jurisdictions. This field helps policymakers, lawyers, and judges adopt best practices, harmonize
laws, and resolve cross-border disputes efficiently.
One key application is in treaty law, where countries enter agreements such as bilateral
investment treaties (BITs), extradition treaties, or trade agreements. These treaties often include
dispute resolution clauses, investor protections, or obligations to surrender fugitives.
Understanding comparative frameworks ensures that states comply with international obligations
while protecting domestic interests. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Another important area is judicial decision-making, where courts refer to international
precedents, foreign judgments, and global conventions to interpret laws and resolve disputes.
Principles like comity of nations allow domestic courts to respect foreign judicial decisions,
fostering mutual legal recognition and cooperation. Similarly, doctrines such as reciprocity and
sovereign immunity guide states in interactions with foreign nationals, foreign governments, or
international organizations.
Comparative International Law also addresses emerging issues, including cybercrime, intellectual
property, environmental regulation, and transnational commercial disputes. Courts and
legislators increasingly rely on comparative studies to craft policies that balance national
sovereignty with global obligations. The field emphasizes harmonization, predictability, and
fairness in international legal practice, enabling states to navigate conflicts of law while
maintaining domestic legal integrity.
